title: Transactional hybrid routing design notes: Anycast + GeoDNS + regional preference
content:
Overview:

This note collects design sketches and operational heuristics for a transactional hybrid steering approach that blends Anycast + GeoDNS + per-request regional preference metadata. The goal: low-latency first-packet routing for most traffic (Anycast), with deterministic region affinity and controlled failover semantics using a light control plane and DNS as a fallback / tiered policy enforcement mechanism.

Motivation / problem statement:
- Anycast gives us single-packet fast-path but is coarse: BGP-level routing decisions cannot express per-customer or per-session preferences.
- GeoDNS provides fine-grained region preference and tiered failover, but DNS TTLs and client resolver caching make it slow to react and harder to maintain single-packet latency.
- Customers require both: sub-100ms p99 for US/Europe, and predictable regional isolation (data residency, latency guarantees) and graceful failover for region outages.
- Need control-plane primitives that can express transactional affinity (for the duration of a session or a short TTL) and coordinate Anycast-driven fast-paths with DNS-driven steering as durable policy.

Sketch: transactional hybrid steering (high-level)
- Fast-path: Anycast front (L3/L4) to nearest egress POP. Front proxies (edge) are lightweight and forward requests to regional clusters.
- Policy plane: Control plane publishes short-lived "affinity tokens" and region preference hints (headers) that clients or edge proxies can use to keep requests pinned during an in-flight session.
- Durable policy: GeoDNS continues to represent the authoritative region preference/primary->secondary ordering with moderate TTLs (30s-120s) for persistent client resolvers and long-lived flows (e.g., SDK/embedded resolvers).
- Fallback: When edge detects region-level degradation it triggers a transactional failover flow: emit token -> probe candidate regions -> shift affinity token to new region -> update metrics and, if needed, escalate to DNS (lower TTL + reorder records) for broader client population.

Key behavioral invariants we want:
1) No blackholes: any request that reaches an edge must get either a local serving path or a clear, deterministic redirect/fallback.
2) Bounded divergence: in steady state regional preference changes must converge within an operator-configured window (e.g., 60–180s) for most users.
3) Minimize cross-region tail latency spikes caused by mid-session rebinds.
4) Observability-first: every affinity transition must emit traces/metrics with enough metadata to reconstruct per-request routing decisions.

Control plane primitives
- Affinity Token (string): opaque token issued by control plane for a given customer/session pairing. Contains TTL (seconds), target-region, and policy-id. Tokens are cryptographically signed; edges cache and honor until TTL expires or explicit revoke.
- Region Scorecard: time-series of health/capacity/latency for each region per service. Scores are computed from probes and production telemetry; published every 5–15s to routing controllers.
- Transactional Roll (idempotent): a control-plane message that atomically flips a small population (selector) from region A -> region B with rollback metadata. Used for canary/failover.
- Probe directive: lightweight instruction to edge to run a special TCP/HTTP probe against a target region and report results (used during transactional failover).

Control plane APIs (informal)
- publishAffinity(customer_id, session_id, preferred_region, ttl, policy_id) -> signed-token
- revokeAffinity(token) -> immediate revoke event propagated to edge caches (push)
- proposeRoll(selector_expression, target_region) -> roll_id; followed by commitRoll(roll_id) or abortRoll(roll_id)
- getRegionScore(service, region) -> score snapshot

Edge behavior (runtime)
- On new incoming connection/request, edge checks for client-supplied affinity token (header or cookie). If present and valid, route to token.target_region. If absent, consult local heuristic: anycast-local, region-preference-table, and sticky-cache by client-ip/req-hash.
- On upstream errors or degraded latency (configurable thresholds), edge triggers transactional failover workflow:
  1) mark local route as degraded (Probe-Degraded) and start local ephemeral local-backoff timer (randomized).
  2) attempt probe directives against top N alternative regions (N default 2).
  3) if probe success -> publishAffinity(control-plane) for the affected selector and return new token to client (via header) to pin subsequent requests.
  4) if probes fail -> start DNS-tier escalation: emit event to control plane to reduce TTL and re-order GeoDNS records for global population.
- Token revocation: edges accept explicit revokes and honor TTL expirations. Revokes are pushed via control-plane SSE or ephemeral pub/sub channel.

State machine (per-route) - simple four-state model:
- Healthy: normal routing. low probe frequency.
- Probe-Degraded: observed p95/p99 or error-rate breach. edge runs directed probes and emits events.
- Local-Eject: local router stops sending traffic to local pool (for selected customers) and returns 503/303 or reroutes to affinity-provisioned region. Token issued.
- Global-Eject: control plane escalated; DNS re-ordering / TTL changes activate for broad population.

Tradeoffs & rationale:
- Why tokens and not sticky BGP? BGP/Anycast cannot carry per-customer state reliably. Tokens give a fine-grained, low-overhead mechanism for per-request steering without disrupting global BGP tables.
- Why keep GeoDNS? Some resolvers and long-lived clients never see token changes; using DNS as the broader, slower-tier ensures any large-scale reconfiguration reaches them eventually. Also useful for customers that manage outbound egress rules by DNS.
- Consistency window: tokens give us a short-term, near-instant consistency (edges can honor immediately). DNS gives eventual consistency for the rest of the world. Must explicitly design for two-tier consistency semantics.

Telemetry and signals to drive decisions
- Per-region time-series: p50/p95/p99 latency, error-rate, saturation (CPU/GPU util), queue-length, token-accept-fraction.
- Edge-level probes: active probing latency and success.
- Control-plane audit log: token issuance, revocation, roll proposals/commits.
- Client-observed metrics: SDKs can emit client telemetry (if customer opts-in) to help measure XA (cross-affinity) effects.

Operational playbook (short)
- Small outage in region X: edges mark degraded -> probes succeed for region Y -> token issued for in-flight sessions -> local rollback timer set (10–30s). If stable, commit roll and instruct DNS to reorder primary to Y with TTL 60s for 5 minutes, then increase TTL back.
- Complete DC outage: immediate Global-Eject; issue DNS reorder + low TTL (30s) + set revoke events for tokens pinned to region X. Kick off capacity redistribution jobs.
- Flapping detection: if region toggles back/forth within 120s, increase hysteresis and require operator confirmation for DNS-level escalations.

Testing & experiments
- Synthetic canary: route 1% of traffic via proposed transactional flow; measure cross-region tail, request success rate, and percent of requests that required DNS escalation.
- Chaos test: eject a region's edge nodes (simulate network partition) and assert no more than X% of requests drop and all tokens eventually revoked.
- Load test: validate token issuance rate at expected scale (tokens per second), size of push channels for revokes.

Edge cases / open questions (action items)
- Q: Where/how should affinity tokens be encoded for non-HTTP (raw TCP/gRPC without header rewrite)?
  A: Consider using initial connection metadata (TLS ALPN extension) or short-lived SRV-like endpoints. Need infra experiments.
- Q: How do we prevent token amplification and abuse if clients intentionally replay tokens?
  A: Sign tokens tied to customer_id and session_hash + nonce; edges rate-limit token acceptance per origin IP.
- Q: When should DNS TTLs be reduced automatically versus operator-only?
  A: Start operator-mediated for first-year rollout; move to automatic on maturity. Add kill-switch.
- Q: Cost model: token churn and probe volume add overhead. What budget (tokens/sec, probes/sec/region) is acceptable?
  Action: finance + platform to propose target overhead per 1M reqs.

Rollout plan (phases)
- Phase 0 (lab): implement token format, edge token acceptance, local probe directive mocks. Internal integration tests.
- Phase 1 (canary): 1% traffic for non-critical customers, operator-triggered DNS toggles disabled. Collect observability.
- Phase 2 (opt-in customers): expose policy to a subset of customers who want deterministic failover semantics.
- Phase 3 (global): automatic failover and DNS escalation enabled for core services, with operator thresholds and SLOs.

Action items (short term)
- Implement minimal token signing library and edge acceptance path (Evan) - PR: routing-protos#412.
- Add Region Scoreboard endpoint and publish format (Lena).
- Draft probe directive wire format and SSE push channel for revokes (Omar).
- Run controlled chaos test in staging and document results (Sofia).

Notes to self / miscellaneous:
- Watch out for IPv6 resolver behavior and DNS64 interactions — some mobile resolvers aggressively cache AAAA lookups.
- Consider client SDK helper that automatically persists token and replays it on reconnect to avoid unnecessary DNS resolution.
- Keep life-cycle of tokens short (30–300s) to limit stale pinned population.

References and related tickets:
- PLAT-8421: affinity token RFC (draft)
- GH PR routing-protos#412: prototype token signing implementation
- Confluence: Hybrid Routing Overview (link above)

Open design questions to review in next sync:
- Token encoding for non-HTTP, TTL budgets, DNS escalation thresholds, operator UI for 'force-eject' vs. automatic.

End of note.

(Working doc — contains sketches and TODOs; not yet finalized. Will convert selected sections into an RFC after engineering sync.)
